title: Meet Kestrel & Pine
basis: Reconstructed from the published page (posts/meet-kestrel-and-pine/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the published page, in its order; tables, figures and callouts are recorded as evidence of the paragraph they follow. Intent outcome, the journal's acceptance criteria, thesis and role are copied unchanged from journal-spec.json. It is a contract, not a description: the places where the published page does not do what the contract asks are listed under open_questions, each beginning 'Published text against this spec'. Revised on 2026-11-12 after the flow rubric: the order of ideas was changed where the decision log says so, and the page was revised to match.

know: Kestrel & Pine at a glance: a fictional outdoor brand with €48 million revenue in 2026, four business lines, three countries, six stores, 1,100 wholesale accounts and three marketplaces.
The January 2027 landscape: thirteen systems named by role, no order management and no product information system, and a stock chain that can run two hours behind.
The ten incidents by name, each with its pattern, and the eight Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Eva's order #1072455 and the four other recurring examples, whose facts do not change between chapters.
believe: Kestrel & Pine's problems are in the joins: every system works, and eight of the ten incidents are one fact in several systems with no agreed owner.
Keeping the platform and deciding ownership first follows from what failed; the platform is not what failed.
can_do: Follow any chapter's opening scene without a re-introduction of the company, its people or its systems.
Look up a figure, a person, an incident or a Waypoint decision when a chapter cites it.
Explain an incident as a named pattern acting on this landscape.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture who have just joined a merchant, a vendor or an agency: engineers, product managers, analysts, consultants and leaders. Most of all the engineer or architect who, like Noor Visser, has to decide about systems they did not choose; the page is written at her altitude.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side.
Roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.
The book's claim that a commerce platform is the whole set of systems that make and keep promises, the four scale stages by name and Kestrel & Pine in one paragraph (introduction).
The names of the sixteen failure patterns, and the Kestrel & Pine incidents used one at a time to illustrate them (where-commerce-platforms-go-wrong).
does_not_know: WMS, ERP, POS, PSP, OMS, PIM, EDI, DESADV, SSCC, iPaaS, GTIN, SKU, 3PL, SaaS, Peppol, D2C, B2B.
Available-to-promise, system of record, idempotent handling, event, reconciliation, tenant, click-and-collect.

thesis.question: Which company do the book's examples come from, and what state are its systems in?
thesis.claim: The examples come from Kestrel & Pine, a fictional outdoor brand with thirteen working systems: orders begin in four, product data sits in four places, warehouse stock passes along a chain of four, and no hub holds orders or products. Eight of its ten incidents are one problem, a fact with several copies and no agreed owner; its 2027 program, Waypoint, names owners first, adds the missing hubs and keeps its commerce platform.
thesis.disputed_by: The reading that a merchant with an oversell, double refunds and drifting prices has ten separate problems, or has outgrown its commerce platform and should replace it.
thesis.so_what: The reader can take each chapter's scene as one more view of a single landscape, check any figure against this page, and ask of each Waypoint decision what the equivalent ownership decision would be in their own company.
thesis.how_why: Each system was bought for the stage the company was in and connected when the need arose. Stock is copied on a schedule from the WMS through the ERP and the platform to the marketplace connector, so every channel can sell a unit for up to two hours after it left the shelf. On Black Friday the platform held and that chain did not.

supporting_claims.claim: Kestrel & Pine is a fictional composite of a growing omnichannel brand, whose four business lines and channels place different demands on its systems.
Each system was bought for the stage the company was in and connected when the need arose, so every system works on its own.
Orders, product data and stock each live in several systems, with no order hub, no product hub and a stock chain that can run two hours behind.
Eight of the ten incidents are one problem: a fact with several copies, no agreed owner and no reliable way for the copies to learn of a change.
Waypoint names an owner for each fact first, adds the missing hubs second and keeps the platform, because the joins failed and the platform did not.
The company's figures, people, incidents and worked examples are fixed in one record, so any chapter can cite them without introducing them again.

role.contribution: Supplies the one merchant, with fixed figures, incidents and decisions, that every chapter's scene and worked example draws on, and performs the part's closing.

flow.rationale: Each section supplies what the next one uses. The glance gives the four business lines; the history says at which stage each system arrived and names every system once, with a gloss, so that the catalog, the channels and the volumes can use those names; each of those three ends on or contains a copy of a fact (product data in four places, store stock copied nightly, a two-hour stock delay in the volumes table). The volumes close the account of the business because they count what flows through the channels; before the channels the figures would have nothing to be counted in. The people come before the systems because the landscape is told as what Noor Visser found and its table names owners (Ruben Alves, the agency, the ERP partner): met first, they are known when the table uses them. The landscape then gathers the copies already seen into two gaps and one stock chain, and the incidents follow it directly, because each incident's mechanism is the landscape's; with the cast between them, as the page first had it, the stock chain was explained and then left for a page. Waypoint follows the incidents because its decisions answer them, and the recurring examples come last because four of the five happen while Waypoint runs and test its priorities. Moving the incidents before the landscape would put ten failures in front of a reader who has not met the stock chain; moving Waypoint before the incidents would present eight decisions as a shopping list. A last short section says how chapters use the record, and the conclusion draws the preface together.

hook.content: The previous page used Kestrel & Pine's incidents one at a time, each to illustrate one failure pattern. This page gives the merchant whole, so that the same incidents can be read as the history of one landscape.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader has met Kestrel & Pine in one paragraph of the introduction and in the incidents the patterns page used one at a time, and will meet a Kestrel & Pine scene at the top of every chapter.
bridge.to_topic: This page gives the company whole and once: an invented composite whose catalog, people, systems and incidents are kept consistent, so that one architectural decision can be seen to affect the next.

thesis_statement.text: Every system at Kestrel & Pine works. But orders begin in four systems, product data is kept in four places and warehouse stock is copied along a chain of four, with no hub for orders or for product data. Eight of the ten incidents come from that: a fact with several copies and no agreed owner. Waypoint, the program approved in 2027, names an owner for each fact first, adds the missing hubs second and keeps the hosted commerce platform it already has.

sections.heading: Kestrel & Pine at a Glance
sections.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine is a profitable, founder-controlled outdoor brand of €48.0 million revenue in 2026, whose four business lines place different demands on the same systems.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the company its fixed baseline figures and the four lines whose differences the landscape has to serve.

flow.rationale: The company, its size, its split into four lines, then what the split means for one jacket: each paragraph divides the figure before it. D2C and B2B are defined in the sentence that introduces the table, because the table's first column uses them. Swap p05 and p06 and the four lines are split before the revenue they divide is stated; put p07 before the table and the jacket's four routes have no lines to belong to.

transition_in.carries_over: The fictional outdoor brand the opening announced.
transition_in.introduces: Its basic facts: founders, ownership, countries, size and business lines.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine B.V. is a founder-controlled outdoor apparel and equipment brand, founded in Arnhem in 2016, that sells mostly own-brand goods in euros in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany.

evidence.what: Founders Mara Lindqvist and Teun Baas keep the majority; fictional investor Veluwe Capital a minority since 2022; own-brand about 75% of revenue, third-party equipment 25%; Belgium since 2020, Germany since 2022.
evidence.shows: Fixes who decides and where the company sells, which later sections rely on (the Waypoint budget, three storefronts).

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2026 it is a profitable mid-sized company with a small technology team: €48.0 million revenue, 310 employees, 14 of them in technology.

evidence.what: Gross margin 54%; EBITDA about €3.4 million; 96 employees in stores, 88 in the warehouse, 126 at head office; technology spend about €2.6 million a year, 5.4% of revenue.
evidence.shows: The company is healthy and its technology budget is modest, so its problems cannot be read as the result of distress.

transition_in.carries_over: The company and its markets.
transition_in.introduces: Its size in 2026: revenue, margin, headcount and technology spend.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four business lines, which the page defines as it names them (D2C, selling through the brand's own storefronts, and B2B, selling to other companies), share the company but place different demands on its systems.

evidence.what: Revenue 2026, orders or transactions, average value and notes per line: online D2C storefronts €27.0M (NL €18.5M, DE €5.5M, BE €3.0M), 293,000 orders, €92; wholesale €12.0M, 9,400 orders, €1,277, 1,100 active accounts, 30-day terms; stores €6.0M, 118,000 transactions, €51, six stores; marketplaces €3.0M, 43,000 orders, €70, bol, Amazon.de and Zalando, other companies' shopping sites.
evidence.shows: The lines differ by more than an order of magnitude in order count and in order value, so one design cannot be sized for all four; the table is the baseline every example quotes.

evidence.what: D2C and B2B are defined in the paragraph before the table that uses them.
evidence.shows: The reader meets the two abbreviations with their meaning, not in a table cell.

transition_in.carries_over: The €48.0 million total.
transition_in.introduces: Its split into four lines, each with its own order count and average value, and the two abbreviations the table uses.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The same jacket sold on a store receipt, in a web order and in a wholesale order needs different prices, payment terms and fulfillment, which is why the four lines cannot be served by one design.

evidence.what: A €51 store receipt, a €92 web order and a €1,277 wholesale order can contain the same jacket.
evidence.shows: One product reaches the systems as three different kinds of sale.

transition_in.carries_over: The table's three average values: €51, €92 and €1,277.
transition_in.introduces: One jacket inside all three, and what each kind of sale demands of the systems.

sections.heading: How Kestrel & Pine Grew, 2016–2027
sections.controlling_idea: Each scale stage Kestrel & Pine passed through left behind a system chosen for that stage, and by 2027 it has thirteen of them to join.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the landscape as the sum of purchases that were each reasonable at the time, which is the 'how' of the thesis.

transition_in.carries_over: The company as it stands in 2026, with its four lines.
transition_in.introduces: How it got there, stage by stage, and which system each stage added.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The history matters because every one of the three scale stages Kestrel & Pine has passed through left a system behind, chosen for the stage it was bought in, and the timeline names each of those systems, with a one-clause gloss, in the row where it arrived.

evidence.what: Year, what happened, stage, one row per year from 2016 to 2027. Starting: the Dutch web shop on a hosted SaaS commerce platform, one payment provider and a 3PL in Tiel (2016), the agency for theme and apps (2017). Growing: the Arnhem store on a cloud POS from a different vendor (2019), Belgium (2020), the Utrecht store, the marketplace connector, the integration platform and GTINs (2021), Germany, Veluwe Capital and Ruben Alves (2022). Omnichannel: the Duiven warehouse on its own WMS, the ERP and the platform's enterprise tier, two stores (2023), Eindhoven and the data warehouse (2024), Antwerp, EDI with Bergzicht and the returns portal (2025), Peppol, the click-and-collect pilot and the Black Friday Oversell (2026), Noor Visser and Waypoint (2027).
evidence.shows: Each row adds systems for the need of that year and stage; reading down the table gives the order in which the landscape was assembled, and one row per year keeps each gloss next to the one or two systems it explains.

evidence.what: The table glosses in one clause each system and term it is the first to name: SaaS, 3PL, theme and apps, POS, the marketplace connector, the integration platform (iPaaS), GTIN, WMS, ERP, the data warehouse, EDI, Bergzicht Outdoor, the returns portal, Peppol, click-and-collect, the Black Friday Oversell and Waypoint.
evidence.shows: Every later section can use these names without a forward reference; the landscape table repeats the glosses for the reader who looks a system up.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The shape of the business, not its revenue, decides the stage: Kestrel & Pine became Omnichannel in 2023, when it had stores, wholesale, marketplaces, three countries and its own warehouse at the same time, and its problems now live in the joins between its thirteen systems.

evidence.what: Revenue bands as rough markers: Starting under about €2 million, Growing to about €20 million, Omnichannel to about €200 million, Group beyond that or several brands.
evidence.shows: At €48 million the company sits low in the Omnichannel band, so it is the shape, not the size, that puts it there.

transition_in.carries_over: The stage column of the table.
transition_in.introduces: What decides a stage: the revenue bands are rough markers, the shape of the business decides.

sections.heading: The Catalog and the Products
sections.controlling_idea: The catalog of 3,400 products and 26,000 variants, with a few recurring prices, has its data kept in four places and no system that owns it.

advances_thesis.how: Fixes the products and prices every example uses and shows the first fact with several copies: product data.

flow.rationale: The whole catalog and its units, then one product and its prices, then where the data about them is kept: the reader has to know what a variant is before four copies of its data mean anything, so the trouble comes last.

transition_in.carries_over: The thirteen systems the history left behind.
transition_in.introduces: What all of them hold data about: products, variants and SKUs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine sells 3,400 products in 26,000 sellable variants, and the book calls one sellable variant a SKU.

evidence.what: A product is 'the Ridgewalker shell jacket, women's', a variant one size in one color; about 17,000 variants active at any time; about 1,200 new variants per season; a GTIN on every own-brand SKU since 2021.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the unit that stock, listings and orders are counted in, and its scale.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The hero product is the Ridgewalker shell jacket, and a few fictional prices recur through the book.

evidence.what: Consumer price including VAT, wholesale price excluding VAT, landed cost: Ridgewalker shell jacket €199, €95, €58; Trailhead fleece €119, €57; merino hiking socks €18, €8.50.
evidence.shows: These are the prices Eva's order, the Price Drift and Bergzicht's reorder are computed from.

evidence.what: VAT is expanded (value-added tax) and landed cost glossed in the sentence that introduces the price table.
evidence.shows: The table's column heads are readable by a newcomer.

transition_in.carries_over: Products and variants in general.
transition_in.introduces: The one product and the few prices the examples use.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Where the product data lives is the first sign of trouble: in January 2027 it is kept in three places, the platform, the ERP and shared spreadsheets, with a fourth copy in the marketplace connector, four copies in all, and there is no PIM.

evidence.what: The platform holds storefront content and variants, the ERP item master purchasing and costs, shared spreadsheets seasonal enrichment and translations, and the marketplace connector a fourth copy for listings.
evidence.shows: One kind of fact has four holders and none is named as the source, the pattern the incidents repeat.

transition_in.carries_over: The products and their prices.
transition_in.introduces: Where the data about them is kept: four copies and no owner.

sections.heading: Channels and Customers
sections.controlling_idea: Each of the four channels reaches its customers through a different system, and each keeps or receives its own copy of stock and orders.

advances_thesis.how: Shows, channel by channel, where orders enter and where stock is copied late or not at all.

flow.rationale: A sentence that ties the four channels to the four business lines, then one labeled paragraph per channel: the two the company sells through itself to consumers (online, stores), then wholesale, then marketplaces, where another company's site and partly another company's warehouse stand between it and the customer. The two wholesale details (the largest account's EDI messages, then the Belgian e-invoices) sit directly after wholesale because they are meaningless without it. Moving marketplaces earlier would introduce the connector's stock push before the reader has seen that store stock is copied only nightly.

transition_in.carries_over: The catalog, and the four business lines of the first table.
transition_in.introduces: The channel each line sells through, to whom, and the system each channel runs on.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The catalog reaches customers through four channels, one for each business line, and no single system serves all four.
Online: three localized storefronts run in one tenant of the platform, and the Dutch one promises next-day delivery from a rule written into the page, not computed from the warehouse's state.

evidence.what: The Netherlands, Belgium in Dutch and French, Germany; one configuration, theme and set of apps; orders before 22:00 delivered tomorrow; iDEAL, card, PayPal, Klarna, Bancontact, Apple Pay. iDEAL is glossed here, at its first use.
evidence.shows: The delivery promise Eva's order later breaks is a static rule, visible here before the example.

transition_in.carries_over: Four channels, each on its own system.
transition_in.introduces: The first: the online storefronts on the platform.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stores: six stores keep their stock in a POS that copies it to the ERP only nightly and has no link to the platform.

evidence.what: About 1,800 variants per store; Arnhem (2019), Utrecht (2021, click-and-collect pilot since 2026), Amsterdam and Nijmegen (2023), Eindhoven (2024), Antwerp (2025, Belgian fiscal receipt rules); the pilot is checked by phone and e-mail; card payments through a separate terminal provider.
evidence.shows: The nightly copy and the missing link are the mechanism of the Store Stock Mirage.

transition_in.carries_over: The online channel on the platform.
transition_in.introduces: The second channel, on a system the platform cannot see.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Wholesale: the 1,100 active accounts send their orders by two routes, 62% through the platform's B2B portal and 38% by e-mail or phone, keyed into the ERP by hand.

evidence.what: 62% of wholesale orders through the B2B portal (company accounts, price lists, payment terms); 38% by e-mail or phone.
evidence.shows: Wholesale orders begin in the platform or in the ERP depending on how the customer orders.

transition_in.carries_over: The stores.
transition_in.introduces: The third channel, whose orders enter two different systems.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The largest wholesale account, the fictional chain Bergzicht Outdoor, has ordered by EDI since 2025, exchanging three messages with Kestrel & Pine: the order, the despatch advice that says what is on which pallet, and the invoice.

evidence.what: 38 shops, a distribution center in Zwolle, €2.1 million a year; EDI is glossed once, in the growth table, and not again here; ORDERS, DESADV (despatch advice, also ASN) and INVOIC named and explained, with EDIFACT and SSCC.
evidence.shows: One account worth more than 4% of revenue orders through a route of its own, and the reader has the despatch advice and the pallet label explained before the landscape table and the ASN Chargeback use them.

transition_in.carries_over: The wholesale accounts and their two ordering routes.
transition_in.introduces: The largest account and a third route, EDI, with its three messages.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Belgian business customers have received Peppol e-invoices since January 2026.

transition_in.carries_over: Electronic documents exchanged with wholesale customers.
transition_in.introduces: A second kind: structured e-invoices over the Peppol network.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Marketplaces: Kestrel & Pine sells on bol, Amazon.de and Zalando through the marketplace connector, and about 40% of its German marketplace units ship from stock held in the marketplace's own fulfillment program, a location outside its control.

evidence.what: bol (NL and BE), Amazon.de, Zalando (DE and NL); the connector publishes listings, pulls orders and pushes stock levels; about 40% of marketplace units for Germany fulfilled by the marketplace's program.
evidence.shows: Orders and stock exist in a fourth place, part of it physically outside the company.

transition_in.carries_over: The wholesale channel and its documents.
transition_in.introduces: The fourth channel, run through a connector that publishes listings, pulls orders and pushes stock.

sections.heading: The Volumes Every Design Is Sized Against
sections.controlling_idea: The 2026 volumes are the fixed, illustrative figures that designs in later chapters are sized against, and two of them, the return rate and the peak hour, rule out sizing by averages.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the numbers every chapter quotes, among them the two-hour stock delay and the four-hour queue at peak.

transition_in.carries_over: The four channels.
transition_in.introduces: How much flows through them in a year, in a peak week and in a peak hour.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Chapters quote these illustrative 2026 figures when they size a queue, a sync interval or a peak plan.

evidence.what: Measure and 2026 value: 293,000 online D2C orders (about 800 a day); 43,000 marketplace orders; 9,400 wholesale orders; 118,000 store transactions; about 17,000 active variants of 26,000; 336,000 parcels plus 9,400 wholesale shipments and 1.9 million units from Duiven; 72,000 return parcels, item return rate 24%, order return rate 19% on D2C, 28% of returns exchanges, 61% resold as new; Black Friday week 31,000 D2C orders, 10.6% of the year's; peak hour Friday 27 November 20:00–21:00, 2,300 orders, 38 per minute, traffic about 41 times an average hour; delays at peak: stock shown to shoppers up to two hours old, orders queued up to four hours before reaching the warehouse, because the WMS vendor's rate limit throttled the flow that created them there.
evidence.shows: One table holds every load figure, so a chapter's sizing argument can be checked against it; the counts of apps and integrations, which describe the systems, are in the landscape table.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Two of the figures deserve a pause because they overturn sizing by averages: the 24% item return rate, and the peak hour, with storefront traffic at about 41 times an average hour and 2,300 orders.

evidence.what: A 24% item return rate: one item comes back for every four shipped.
evidence.shows: The return path carries routine volume, so it has to be designed as a main flow.

evidence.what: Storefront traffic in the peak hour is about 41 times an average hour, and a design that works at 800 orders a day meets 2,300 in one hour, once a year; the pattern The First Snowfall warns about this.
evidence.shows: The average hides the load that breaks the design.

transition_in.carries_over: The table of volumes.
transition_in.introduces: The two rows a designer must not read past, and what each implies.

sections.heading: The People
sections.controlling_idea: The business is run by a small fictional cast, each of whom owns something the architecture depends on, and the reader's stand-in is Noor Visser, who has to decide about systems she did not choose.

advances_thesis.how: Fixes the cast every scene uses and ties each system and fact to a person, which is what 'owner' means in the incidents and in Waypoint; it also introduces Noor, through whose arrival the landscape is told.

transition_in.carries_over: The business as described so far: its lines, catalog, channels and volumes, and the names the timeline has already used (Noor Visser, Ruben Alves, the agency).
transition_in.introduces: The whole cast and what each person owns.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The business described so far is run by a small fictional cast, from Mara Lindqvist, the CEO who holds the Waypoint budget, to Ruben Alves, the agency and the ERP partner, who own its integrations; each owns something the architecture depends on, so most of the book's tensions are between their legitimate goals.

sections.heading: The Systems Landscape in January 2027
sections.controlling_idea: In January 2027 every system in the landscape works, but none holds all orders or all product data, and stock reaches the channels through a chain of copies that can run two hours behind.

advances_thesis.how: States the two gaps and the stock chain, which are the mechanism the thesis attributes the incidents to.

flow.rationale: The assertion first (every system works, two are missing), with the table as its evidence; then the reasoning: what the two missing systems would do, what their absence does to orders and product data, and the one chain of copies behind the largest incident. The stock chain comes last because the figure it is read from is attached to the paragraph before it, and because the next section opens on the incident it produced. Swap p21 and p22 and the reader is told what the two missing systems would do before seeing that they are missing; move p24 before p23 and the stock chain is read before the reader knows orders and product data have no hub either.

transition_in.carries_over: Noor Visser, asked to decide about systems she did not choose.
transition_in.introduces: Those systems as she found them in January 2027.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When Noor Visser arrives in January 2027 she finds a landscape in which every system works, each named here by its role, and two rows of the table have no system at all.

evidence.what: Area, system, since, notes: the platform (2016; three storefronts in one tenant, agency theme, 41 apps of which 6 unused and 3 write stock); the ERP (2023; connector built by the ERP partner); the WMS (2023; orders in from the platform, stock out to the ERP, via the iPaaS); order management: none (orders live in the platform, the connector, the ERP and the POS); product information: none (data in the platform, the ERP, spreadsheets and the connector); the marketplace connector (2021; hourly stock sync); the POS (2019; store stock to the ERP nightly, no link to the platform); the returns portal (2025; refunds through the platform's API); the shipping service (2023); the PSP (2016; separate terminal provider for stores since 2019); the EDI provider (2025; ORDERS, DESADV, INVOIC with Bergzicht; Peppol); the iPaaS plus agency scripts and vendor connectors (2021; 34 integrations, owned by Ruben Alves); the data warehouse and a BI tool (2024; three definitions of 'order'). Each system is glossed in one clause, except the iPaaS, already glossed in the growth table.
evidence.shows: The reader sees every system by role and the two rows, answered 'none', where a fact has four holders.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The table names thirteen systems and two gaps, and the two missing systems explain much of the difficulty: an order management system, which would coordinate orders from every channel with shared states, and a product information management system, which would own descriptions and attributes.

transition_in.carries_over: The table: thirteen systems counted from its rows, and the two rows that say 'none'.
transition_in.introduces: What each missing system would do if it existed.

evidence.what: Thirteen systems, counted after the table: eleven rows name one each, the payments row adds the stores' terminal provider and the data row a BI tool; scripts and connectors between systems are not counted.
evidence.shows: The count the thesis uses can be checked against the table the reader has just read.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Without those two systems, orders begin in four places and product descriptions are maintained four times, because buying a useful system for each new need has left the company without shared ownership.

evidence.what: Figure 1, the January 2027 landscape: four channels create orders in four different systems, stock travels from the WMS to the ERP to the platform to the marketplace connector on a schedule, and no system holds all orders or all product data.
evidence.shows: The two gaps and the stock chain are visible in one picture.

transition_in.carries_over: What an OMS and a PIM would do.
transition_in.introduces: What happens instead, and the cause: one purchase per need, no shared ownership.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The stock sync chain in the middle of the figure is the mechanism behind the Black Friday Oversell: warehouse stock is copied from the WMS to the ERP, the platform and the connector in turn, four copies in all, so a sale can take up to two hours to reduce the number a shopper sees.

evidence.what: The WMS passes its number on a schedule to the ERP, the ERP to the platform, the platform to the connector, and the connector to the marketplaces: four systems, each holding its own copy. A sale at Duiven can take up to two hours to reach Amazon.de, and in that time every channel believes it can still sell the unit.
evidence.shows: The delay comes from scheduled copies, each working as designed.

evidence.what: Figure 2, the Black Friday Oversell: an empty jacket shelf at Duiven at 19:40 while storefront screens still show the jacket in stock from a copy up to two hours old; 1,340 units oversold.
evidence.shows: What the chain did on its worst evening: the shelf and its copies disagree.

sections.heading: The Problems Kestrel & Pine Starts 2027 With
sections.controlling_idea: Every system works and the problems are in the joins: eight of the ten incidents are one fact held in several systems with no agreed owner.

advances_thesis.how: Lists the ten incidents with their numbers, patterns and owning chapters and states what eight of them have in common.

transition_in.carries_over: The landscape Noor found: every system working, two hubs missing, and a stock chain that can run two hours behind.
transition_in.introduces: What that landscape produced: ten incidents, the first of them the oversell the stock chain explains.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When Noor starts, every system in that landscape works and the problems are in the joins: ten incidents, most from 2026 and two from her first weeks, define the position she starts from, all but one an instance of a pattern named on the previous page and each worked in full by the chapter that owns it; they keep the numbers by which chapters cite them.

evidence.what: 1 The Black Friday Oversell (27 November 2026): sold out at Duiven at 19:40, sold elsewhere for up to two hours; 1,340 units oversold, 1,120 orders canceled or delayed, about €96,000; The Phantom Stock and The First Snowfall. 2 The Three-Status Order (December 2026): order #1052877 Delivered in the platform, In picking in the WMS, Not invoiced in the ERP for six days, 11 support tickets; Schrödinger's Order. 3 The Double Refund (January 2027): 212 returns refunded twice, €19,400, most recovered; The Boomerang and The Message in a Bottle. 4 The Price Drift (October 2026): the German storefront at €179 for nine days against €199 elsewhere, 410 orders, about €8,200 of margin; The Price Nobody Can Explain. 5 The ASN Chargeback (Q3 2026): Bergzicht deducted €14,200 for despatch advices that did not match the pallets, because the DESADV came from the ERP's view and not from what the warehouse packed; The Pulled Rug and The Lynchpin.
evidence.shows: Five incidents in which two or three systems held different values of one fact (stock, status, refund, price, shipment contents).

evidence.what: 6 The Store Stock Mirage (December 2026): click-and-collect at Utrecht promised 37 items already sold; The Phantom Stock from the store side. 7 The App That Wrote Stock (March 2026): a pre-order app and the WMS feed both wrote inventory, two weeks of phantom reservations on 600 variants; The Secret Agent and The Spaghetti Junction. 8 The Card-Testing Night (August 2026): 48,000 bot attempts, €2,900 in PSP fees, account paused 40 minutes; a trust failure, not one of the sixteen patterns. 9 The Familiar Stranger: Eva Janssen is four unlinked customer records. 10 The Deprecated Endpoint (February 2027): the connector retired an API version an agency script still read, stock to bol stale for two days; The Pulled Rug.
evidence.shows: The remaining five, each with its figures, its pattern and its owning chapter linked, so a later chapter can cite an incident by name.

evidence.what: Incident 5 uses the despatch advice (DESADV) and the pallet label as the channels section explained them, and adds no definition of its own.
evidence.shows: The incident can be read for its point: the message was built from the wrong system.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Eight of the ten incidents (1 to 7 and 9) are the same problem, a fact (stock, an order's status, a refund, a price, a shipment's contents, a customer's identity) that lives in more than one system with no agreed owner and no reliable way for the copies to learn of a change; the other two, the Card-Testing Night (8) and the Deprecated Endpoint (10), are what the outside world does to a landscape nobody watches as a whole.

transition_in.introduces: What eight of them share and how the other two differ.

sections.heading: The Waypoint Program
sections.controlling_idea: Waypoint answers the incidents in a deliberate order: who owns each fact first, then the missing hubs, then trustworthy copies, with the platform kept because the joins failed and the platform did not.

advances_thesis.how: Presents the eight decisions and reads their order as the argument the thesis ends on.

transition_in.carries_over: Ten incidents, eight of them a fact with no agreed owner.
transition_in.introduces: The program approved in March 2027 to answer them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: To answer the incidents, Mara Lindqvist approved Waypoint in March 2027 on Noor's proposal, €1.1 million over 2027–2028, and its eight decisions are canonical: chapters explain them and never change them.

evidence.what: Decision, what changes, when. W1 Stock ownership: the WMS is the system of record for stock at Duiven, the POS for store stock, marketplace fulfillment stock a tracked external location; an availability service computes available-to-promise per channel from stock events; the sync chain is retired (Q4 2027). W2 One order record: a bought OMS becomes the order hub for every channel, with one state model; the platform keeps checkout and storefront order history (Q4 2027). W3 Product information: a PIM is the system of record for content and attributes; the ERP keeps costs and purchasing (Q3 2027). W4 Stay and surround: no replatforming; OMS, PIM and availability are added beside the SaaS platform; its POS evaluated in 2028 (2027, review 2029). W5 Integration standards: an owner, a contract, idempotent handling and a reconciliation job per integration; stock, orders and prices by events, products by scheduled publication, finance by daily batch (from 2027). W6 EDI compliance: SSCC labels at pack time, DESADV from the WMS pack confirmation (2027). W7 One definition of an order in the data warehouse, owned by the Data Lead (2027). W8 Agent readiness, not agents: product data, availability, delivery promise and order status by API; no shopper-facing AI agent in 2027 (2027).
evidence.shows: Each decision is stated with what changes and when, and system of record, event, available-to-promise, idempotent and reconciliation job are glossed in the cell that first uses them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read by priority instead of by number, the decisions are the argument: Waypoint decides who owns each fact first, then adds the hubs the landscape lacks, then makes the copies trustworthy, and it does not replace the platform because the joins failed and the platform did not.

evidence.what: Ownership (the system-of-record choices in W1, W3 and W7) comes before the hubs that hold what was decided (the availability service in W1, the OMS in W2, the PIM in W3), which come before the integration standards and EDI compliance (W5, W6); W4 keeps the platform, and W8 builds on the result: accurate product data, availability and order status are what a later shopping agent would need. The table lists the decisions by number and its dates do not show this priority.
evidence.shows: A hub bought before ownership is decided would be one more holder of a fact with no agreed owner.

transition_in.carries_over: The eight decisions in the table.
transition_in.introduces: The priority among them, which is not the table's order (owners in W1, W3, W7; the hubs; W5, W6; W4), and why that priority is the point.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The preface's three pages are one argument at three sizes: the ten incidents are instances of the patterns the previous page named, the patterns are promises broken at the joins between systems, and the order of Waypoint's decisions (who owns each fact, then the missing hubs, then trustworthy copies, with the platform kept) is the book's claim written as one company's program.
conclusion.so_what: The reader can open any chapter, take its scene as one more view of a landscape and a list of failures they already know, check any figure against this page, and expect the chapter to explain a decision about ownership and joins, not a product choice.

callback.to: The book's first page, which opened on Eva's order #1072455 and the 1,340 units oversold on Black Friday, and this page's opening statement that the facts are kept consistent so that one decision can be seen to affect the next (p01).
callback.how: The two numbers have returned on this page as the recurring order and as incident 1, now with the landscape that explains them; they mean the same on every page.

takeaway.content: Begin Part I as Noor began her first week: follow one order through every system it touches and ask at each handoff which system made the promise and which one has to keep it.

hand_off.carries_over: Kestrel & Pine with its problems and its program, and the preface's claim that a commerce platform is the set of systems that make and keep promises.
hand_off.introduces: Part I, which takes up the business before the technology: what the promises are, who makes them and who owns the facts behind them, starting from one order followed through every system.

Part I takes up the business before the technology, what the promises are, who makes them and who owns the facts behind them, and it begins where Noor began in her first week: by following one order through every system it touches and asking at each handoff which system made the promise and which one has to keep it.
